title: A Machine with a Name
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 22 of 40
content:
Nick Valentine smoked like someone had told him it was impossible for a synth to get lung cancer and he had taken that as a challenge.

Danse disliked him immediately.

Nick returned the favor with professionalism.

We encountered him in Diamond City while following a lead on stolen Brotherhood equipment. He was leaning against a wall outside the detective agency, hat low, cigarette ember bright beneath the market lights.

“Paladin,” Nick said.

“Synth.”

“Always nice to feel seen.”

I closed my eyes briefly.

“This is going to be a long evening.”

Nick looked at me.

“You traveling with him voluntarily?”

“Usually.”

Danse crossed his arms.

“We’re not here to socialize.”

“No danger of that.”

The stolen equipment turned out to be in the hands of a group of raiders operating near Back Street Apparel. Nick had information. Danse needed it.

This created what I can only describe as tactical politeness.

Nick gave directions.

Danse said thank you as if the words had been requisitioned from a limited supply.

Before we left, Nick said, “Try not to shoot anybody just for having the wrong factory parts.”

Danse’s shoulders went rigid.

I stepped between them.

“Good talk.”

Outside the city, Danse walked in silence for nearly a mile.

Then he said, “You enjoy putting me in these situations.”

“I did not invent Nick Valentine.”

“You could have gotten the information elsewhere.”

“Why?”

“Because he’s an Institute machine.”

“He hates the Institute.”

“That doesn’t change what he is.”

There it was again.

I thought of Amos.

“What is he?” I asked.

Danse gave me an incredulous look.

“A synth.”

“That’s a noun. Try harder.”

“A machine built to imitate a human.”

“He has memories, preferences, friendships, a job, moral opinions, and apparently better manners than you.”

“He was programmed.”

“So were you.”

Danse stopped walking.

The words had come out harsher than I intended.

I held up a hand.

“I mean trained. We’re all shaped by something.”

“That is not the same.”

“No. It isn’t.”

His face remained tight.

I softened my voice.

“But how much difference matters before you decide someone isn’t a person?”

Danse stared at the road.

“I don’t know why you keep pushing this.”

“Because I care what you think.”

That landed harder than the argument.

He looked at me.

“And because one day,” I continued, “I’m afraid your rules are going to ask you to hurt someone who doesn’t deserve it.”

“You think I’m capable of that.”

The hurt in his voice stopped me.

“That’s not what I said.”

“It’s what you meant.”

“No.”

I stepped closer.

“I think you’re capable of choosing differently if you let yourself look at the person in front of you before the category.”

Danse’s jaw worked.

“We have a mission.”

Conversation over.

The raider camp was violent enough to make philosophy irrelevant for an hour.

We recovered the equipment.

On the way back, a mechanical voice called for help from an alley.

A damaged protectron lay beneath fallen masonry.

Danse ignored it.

I stopped.

“What are you doing?”

“It’s a robot.”

“It asked for help.”

“It’s running a programmed emergency routine.”

“Probably.”

I started lifting debris.

Danse stared at me.

Then swore and helped.

We freed the protectron.

It thanked us and wandered away announcing municipal safety regulations.

Danse watched it go.

“This proves nothing.”

“I didn’t say it did.”

“Then why are you smiling?”

“Because you helped.”

“Because you were going to injure yourself moving that slab alone.”

“Whatever you need to tell yourself.”

He gave me the look.

Back in Diamond City, Nick was still outside his office.

We returned his borrowed map.

Danse hesitated.

Then said, “Your information was accurate.”

Nick raised one eyebrow.

“Careful. Keep talking like that and people will think we’re friends.”

“We are not.”

“Good. I have a reputation.”

I laughed.

Danse almost did.

Almost.

As we walked away, he said, “I still don’t trust him.”

“I know.”

“But I acknowledge he acted in good faith.”

I looked at him.

“That’s not nothing.”

“No.”

He slipped his hand briefly against the small of my back to guide me through the crowd.

The touch lasted only a second.

A machine with a name, I thought.

A man with rules.

A future neither of us could see coming.

Nick found us again before we left Diamond City.

Not because he wanted to continue the argument.

Because somebody had shot at him from the upper stands.

The bullet had clipped the side of his face, tearing synthetic skin away and exposing metal beneath. Nick appeared more irritated than hurt.

Danse stopped dead.

The damage made every abstract thing between them visible.

Machine.

Person.

Both, perhaps.

Nick touched the torn edge of his cheek.

“Don’t suppose either of you know a good seamstress.”

I winced.

Danse stared.

“What happened?” he asked.

Nick raised one eyebrow.

“Concern, Paladin?”

“Threat assessment.”

“Of course.”

A second shot struck the wall behind us.

Threat assessment became immediate.

Danse grabbed Nick by the coat and pulled him behind a concrete stall while I ducked the other way. The shooter fired again from a balcony.

Danse could have let Nick take the round.

He did not.

He moved before belief had time to vote.

We chased the gunman through two alleys and lost him near the city gate. By the time we returned, Nick was sitting on an overturned bucket while Ellie fussed over the damage to his face.

Danse hovered several feet away.

Nick looked at him.

“Saved my hide.”

“I prevented a hostile shooter from completing an attack inside a civilian settlement.”

“Right. My mistake.”

Danse crossed his arms.

Nick’s visible mechanical eye clicked as it focused.

“Funny thing about reflexes,” he said. “Sometimes they know what you believe before you do.”

Danse’s jaw tightened.

“I would have done the same for anyone.”

“That’s sort of my point.”

The silence that followed was almost impressive.

Ellie looked at me.

I looked at the ceiling.

This was not my argument to win.

Nick eventually stood.

“Thanks anyway, soldier.”

Danse nodded once.

“You’re welcome.”

Not *synth*.

Not *machine*.

You.

We left the agency a few minutes later.

Danse made it halfway through the market before speaking.

“I acted before identifying him.”

“You identified a person being shot at.”

“I identified an ally in the immediate situation.”

“Okay.”

He frowned at my lack of argument.

“That does not prove personhood.”

“I didn’t say it did.”

“You usually say something.”

“I’m trying a radical new strategy where I let you think.”

“That sounds manipulative.”

“Probably.”

We stopped near the noodle stand. Steam rose into the evening air.

Danse watched people move through the market.

“What if he believes he’s a person because he was designed to?”

“Then he believes it.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the only one I have.”

He looked frustrated.

I leaned against the counter.

“What would convince you?”

“That a synth is human?”

“That a synth is a person.”

Danse opened his mouth.

Closed it.

He had standards for threats, orders, maintenance, marksmanship, rank. He had no field test for personhood.

“I don’t know,” he admitted.

The words cost him.

I nodded.

“That’s somewhere to start.”

He looked at me sharply.

“I am not changing my position.”

“I know.”

“You sound pleased.”

“I am.”

“Why?”

“Because ‘I don’t know’ is more honest than pretending the answer is easy.”

Danse stared out at the market again.

A child ran past chasing a ball. A ghoul trader argued over ammunition. Nick’s silhouette moved behind the agency window.

“I still think synths represent a grave threat,” he said.

“That’s not an irrational fear. The Institute literally replaces people.”

He looked at me.

“You agree?”

“I agree the Institute is terrifying. I don’t agree that every person they build inherits the guilt.”

Danse’s gaze returned to the window.

“We may never agree on this.”

“Maybe.”

I nudged his shoulder.

“You still saved Nick.”

“He was standing in my line of responsibility.”

“That phrase is going to do incredible work for you emotionally.”

His mouth twitched despite himself.

Nick had left us with one final remark.

“Funny thing about names,” he said, adjusting his hat over the damage to his face. “They’re mostly promises people agree to keep calling you.”

Danse had frowned at that.

He frowned at it for the next mile too.

“What?” I finally asked.

“Nothing.”

“That’s become your least convincing word.”

He glanced at me. “Valentine talks too much.”

“Yes.”

“He also makes imprecise philosophical claims.”

“Also yes.”

A pause.

“I understand what he meant.”

I did not push.

The fact that he had kept thinking about it was enough.

On the road back to the airport, Danse stopped beside a ruined storefront.

“What?” I asked.

He looked at me with something almost vulnerable.

“If I ever become the person you think I could be… don’t let me pretend I was always that person.”

The request startled me.

“I won’t.”

“I mean it.”

“I know.”

He nodded.

Then we kept walking.

Neither of us understood yet how cruelly literal that promise would become.
